content: Indoor residual spraying (IRS) is one of the two primary methods for large-scale malaria prevention, alongside insecticide-treated mosquito nets (ITNs). Historically, IRS has been effective in reducing malaria transmission in various regions worldwide. However, its health effects have not been adequately quantified, which is essential for comparing its efficacy with other vector control interventions. The objective of this study was to measure the impact of IRS alone and to compare its effects with ITNs on key malaria-related parameters. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and others, up to September 2009. Researchers, organizations, and insecticide manufacturers were also contacted for additional data. The study included cluster randomized controlled trials (RCTs), controlled before-and-after studies (CBA), and interrupted time series (ITS) that compared IRS with no IRS or ITNs. Studies focusing on special populations or using non-WHO-recommended insecticides or dosages were excluded. Two authors independently reviewed the trials for inclusion, extracted data, assessed the risk of bias, and analyzed the results. Confidence intervals (CIs) were adjusted for clustering where possible. The studies were categorized into those comparing IRS with no IRS and those comparing IRS with ITNs, further stratified by malaria endemicity. IRS versus No IRS Stable Malaria (Entomological Inoculation Rate (EIR) > 1): In a randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted in Tanzania, IRS reduced malaria re-infection rates in children following treatment, with a protective efficacy (PE) of 54%. However, the reduction in malaria case incidence, assessed through passive surveillance, was marginal in children aged 1–5 years (PE 14%) and negligible in children older than 5 years (PE -2%). Malaria prevalence in the IRS group was slightly lower but not statistically significant (PE 6%). Mean hemoglobin levels were higher in the IRS group, with a mean difference of 0.85 g/dL. A controlled before-and-after (CBA) study in Nigeria demonstrated that IRS provided protection against malaria prevalence during the wet season (PE 26%; 95% CI 20–32%) but not during the dry season (PE 6%; 95% CI -4 to 15%). An interrupted time series (ITS) study in Mozambique showed a substantial reduction in malaria prevalence over seven years, from 60–65% to 4–8%, with a weighted PE of 74% (95% CI 72–76%). Unstable Malaria (EIR < 1): Two RCTs demonstrated that IRS reduced the incidence of all malaria infections, with a PE of 31% in India and 88% (95% CI 69–96%) in Pakistan. By species, IRS reduced the incidence of Plasmodium falciparum (PE 93%, 95% CI 61–98%) and Plasmodium vivax (PE 79%, 95% CI 45–90%) in Pakistan. Malaria prevalence also decreased, with a PE of 76% in Pakistan and 28% in India. For P. falciparum, the PE was 92% in Pakistan and 34% in India. For P. vivax, the PE was 68% in Pakistan, but no significant impact was observed in India (PE -2%). IRS versus ITNs Stable Malaria (EIR > 1): Only one RCT was conducted in a stable transmission area (Tanzania). When comparing parasitological re-infection rates through active surveillance, ITNs appeared to perform better than IRS, but the difference was not statistically significant (risk ratio IRS:ITN = 1.22). No difference was observed in malaria incidence among children aged 1–5 years (risk ratio = 0.88, favoring IRS). Similarly, no significant differences were found in malaria prevalence or hemoglobin levels. Unstable Malaria (EIR < 1): Two studies compared IRS and ITNs. In one study, malaria incidence and prevalence were higher in the IRS group compared to the ITN group. In India, malaria incidence was higher in the IRS group (risk ratio IRS:ITN = 1.48). In South Africa, the risk ratio was 1.34, but the unadjusted CIs included 1, indicating no significant difference. For malaria prevalence, ITNs provided better protection against any infection compared to IRS in India (risk ratio IRS:ITN = 1.70). This was also true for P. falciparum (risk ratio IRS:ITN = 1.78) and P. vivax (risk ratio IRS:ITN = 1.37). Authors' Conclusions Historical and programmatic evidence has established the effectiveness of IRS in reducing malaria transmission. However, the number of high-quality trials is insufficient to quantify its impact across different transmission settings. Evidence from randomized comparisons confirms that IRS reduces malaria incidence in unstable transmission areas, but data from stable transmission settings are limited. Preliminary findings suggest that ITNs may provide better protection than IRS in unstable areas, but more trials are needed to directly compare the two interventions and to evaluate their combined effects. Future studies should ideally focus on areas without prior malaria control activities to better assess the standalone impact of IRS.
